detailed_summary: This paper presents Amatlas, a distributed Union-Find (UF) decoder for surface codes that eliminates the need for a central controller and uses a two-dimensional processing element (PE) array. Prior distributed UF decoders map the three-dimensional decoding graph onto a 3D PE array with a central controller that synchronizes all PEs at every stage, which scales poorly on planar hardware. Amatlas instead assigns one PE to each stabilizer on the 2D qubit lattice and stores all measurement rounds in local memory, so every link connects adjacent PEs. Each PE advances every clock cycle without array-wide synchronization; the clock is the only global signal. The RTL implementation fits a VCU129 FPGA up to code distance 25, achieving an average decoding time of 462 ns per round at a physical error rate of 0.1% under circuit-level noise. The decoder achieves a threshold of 0.72%, compared to 0.78% for standard UF decoding under the same noise model.
key_contributions: Amatlas: a 2D PE array architecture for UF decoding that eliminates the central controller and array-wide synchronization, using only a global clock.
Mapping of the 3D decoding graph onto a 2D PE array by assigning one PE per stabilizer and storing all measurement rounds in local memory, ensuring all links are between adjacent PEs.
Demonstration via RTL implementation that Amatlas fits a VCU129 FPGA up to code distance 25, with average decoding time of 462 ns per round at 0.1% physical error rate.
Characterization of threshold: 0.72% under circuit-level noise, compared to 0.78% for standard UF decoding, quantifying the performance cost of the distributed architecture.
methodology_analysis: The core methodological innovation is the architectural mapping of the 3D space-time decoding graph onto a 2D array of PEs. Instead of using a 3D PE array with a central controller, Amatlas assigns each stabilizer on the 2D qubit lattice to a dedicated PE. Each PE stores the syndromes for all measurement rounds in its local memory, effectively embedding the time dimension into memory rather than into physical PE dimensions. This ensures that all communication links connect only adjacent PEs in the 2D array, which is compatible with planar hardware. The decoder operates without any array-wide synchronization: each PE advances on every clock cycle based on local state and messages from neighbors, with the clock being the only global signal. This asynchronous, local-control design avoids the scalability bottleneck of a central controller. The authors implement the design in RTL and evaluate it on a VCU129 FPGA under circuit-level noise, measuring decoding latency and threshold.
results_analysis: The RTL implementation of Amatlas fits on a VCU129 FPGA up to a code distance of 25, which is a significant scale for a real-time decoder. At a physical error rate of 0.1%, the average decoding time is 462 ns per round. The threshold is measured at 0.72% under circuit-level noise, which is lower than the 0.78% reported for standard UF decoding under the same noise model. This 0.06 percentage point reduction in threshold represents the performance cost of the distributed, asynchronous architecture. The results demonstrate that a 2D PE array without a central controller can achieve real-time decoding for large code distances, but with a modest threshold penalty.
strengths: Eliminates the central controller and array-wide synchronization, enabling scalable distributed decoding on planar hardware.
Achieves real-time decoding (462 ns per round) for code distance up to 25 on a single FPGA, demonstrating practical feasibility.
Provides a clear quantitative comparison of threshold (0.72% vs. 0.78%) against standard UF decoding, honestly reporting the performance trade-off.
limitations: The threshold is reduced from 0.78% to 0.72%, indicating a non-negligible performance degradation compared to centralized UF decoding.
The evaluation is limited to a single FPGA device (VCU129) and a specific noise model; scalability to larger code distances or other hardware platforms is not explored.
The paper does not provide a detailed comparison with other distributed decoder architectures in terms of resource usage, latency, or threshold, making it difficult to assess relative advantages.
connections_to_research: This work is directly relevant to quantum physics and quantum computing, specifically fault-tolerant quantum computing with surface codes. It addresses the critical engineering challenge of real-time decoding, which is essential for scaling quantum computers. The architectural innovations in distributed decoding and the threshold analysis contribute to the practical realization of fault-tolerant quantum computation. Researchers interested in quantum error correction, hardware architectures for quantum control, and the intersection of quantum physics with classical computing will find this paper valuable.
overall_assessment: Amatlas presents a novel and practical architecture for distributed surface code decoding that removes the central controller bottleneck. The RTL implementation and FPGA demonstration at code distance 25 with sub-microsecond decoding time are impressive. The threshold penalty of 0.06% is modest and acceptable for many applications. The paper is well-structured and provides concrete results, though it could benefit from broader comparisons and exploration of scalability. Overall, it is a significant contribution to the field of quantum error correction hardware, bridging the gap between theoretical decoders and practical implementations.
